column2: Act Five
Dragon Shadow
At that moment lightning tore the sky apart, and in its glare the black shape twisted like a raging dragon.
Selma's knees gave way, and she collapsed onto the deck. Countless lectures had taught her that this race existed in the world, but she had never once seen one reveal itself.
It was a miracle: a dragon breaking out of the water and ascending into the sky. All this wind and rain had come to welcome this magnificent moment.
A deluge of information poured into Ye Sheng's brain through his Snakes, as if the entire Pacific Ocean were flowing backward into the Yangtze.

His brain was now a computer overclocked to the point of overheating. The pain was so immense it threatened to tear him apart. Among the information was a three-dimensional map. The enormous bronze city, perhaps the true White Emperor City of history, was completely transparent before him.

The colossal mechanism cast two thousand years ago had come to life. Apparently solid bronze walls split open, and millions of cubic meters of air escaped through the cracks with shrill howls, while the surging water below forced its way in to fill the void. A spiderweb of bronze corridors rotated and reconnected, like a revolver's cylinder turning as it fired, bringing a fresh chamber into line with the barrel.

The escape route changed every second. Ye Sheng was going out of his mind. He had his map, but... imagine looking at a map of Beijing and discovering that Chaoyang District was slowly moving toward Fangshan, while Haidian slid clockwise to occupy Chaoyang's position. The East Third Ring Road broke away from the North Third Ring Road and moments later joined the South Second Ring! Any driver who had half an hour to get out of the city would have to be crazy not to go crazy.

Behind them, a twenty-meter-high bronze wall was slowly toppling, like the vault of heaven tipping sideways. Aki swam forward with her arm hooked around Ye Sheng's neck. He was almost completely spent.

Aki's mind was a jumble. She remembered when they had first enrolled. Ye Sheng had been eighteen, fresh from China, with two thick, sweeping black eyebrows. The best swimmer in their class, he had become captain of the sailing team in his second year and won the Golden Fleece Cup back from the University of Chicago. The girls in their class had certainly noticed him. His favorite pastime was making fun of Aki. Every swimming class, while Aki the clumsy duck was still halfway through her thousand-meter warm-up, Ye Sheng would already have finished his thousand meters and a spot of sunbathing besides. Wearing nothing but swim trunks, his broad shoulders and long arms bare, he would turn his back on her and slap his own butt, saying obnoxious things like, "Do Japanese people swim so slowly because their legs are short?" Then his face would suddenly fill with despair. "We're going to be partners someday. Am I doomed to die underwater?" He could not possibly have been more infuriating.

The bronze wall struck the water and sent up a tremendous wave that hurled them against the opposite wall. Aki turned just in time to shield Ye Sheng in her arms. The impact nearly dislocated her lumbar vertebrae. Gritting her teeth, she clutched the man, weak as a baby in her arms, while a thread of blood seeped from the corner of her mouth.

When had protecting Ye Sheng become a habit? Back then, to get back at him for his teasing, she had pointed straight at his nose and shouted, "If you drown someday, don't expect me to save you!" How had things turned out this way?
The Key! Ye Sheng shouted hoarsely.
Carried by the Snakes' electric current, his cry reverberated through the Moniach's cabin like a wounded wolf's last howl.
Mans froze. "Yes! The Key! The Key will know what to do!" he shouted.

The sleeping baby was rushed to the forward cabin. The instant he was set before the display, his eyes miraculously opened. A faint light flowed in their depths. He reached out a chubby finger and slid it across the enormous screen, his gaze sweeping over every corner of the map.
Come on, baby. It's up to you! Mans watched his finger intently.
His fingertip rested against the screen, slowly descending... descending. The light faded from his eyes, and he became an ordinary baby again. Suddenly he burst into loud sobs!
Mans's heart plunged. Could it be... there was no way out?

Ye Sheng's eyes flew open, a faint golden glow filling his pupils. As the Key's crying reached him, a clear red line suddenly appeared on the shifting map in his mind. Downward. Straight down, through gaps between walls, through corridors, even through solid bronze walls, finally emerging from the bottom.
That's the exit! Ye Sheng understood!

The Key had grasped the pattern governing the bronze city's movement. They only had to keep going down. When they reached those thick, solid walls, the city's machinery would open new passages through them. This was their last escape route, but they had to be fast. If they were too slow, they would be sealed inside a dead end or crushed flat in a slowly closing gap.
The Key was crying out of fear, not sadness. The Key was urging them to hurry!
Directly below. Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku preparing to exit! Ye Sheng's voice returned to the forward cabin.
Directly below? Mans paused. Only now did he notice the track the Key's finger had left on the screen: a straight line leading out through the bottom of the bronze city.
Forty-five meters away! Selma said. "Three minutes of oxygen left!"
Add the time they can swim on a held breath, and at their speed they'll just make it! Mans's voice was so jubilant it almost soared into the sky.

Ye Sheng ended his Yanling, and his strength returned. He turned to take Aki's hand, but she did not move. She switched on the dim light inside her helmet so that he could see her face. Her lips moved, but he could not hear her. The signal cable connecting them had also snapped.
We won't make it. We don't have enough oxygen, Aki said, opening her faceplate. The extremely low oxygen level made her cough violently.
Ye Sheng glanced at the remaining oxygen: enough for three minutes. Add his ability to stay active underwater for five minutes without breathing, and they had just enough to swim out.
It's enough. He opened his faceplate too.

It isn't. Aki shook her head. Tears crept slowly down her cheeks. "Let's stay here. I want to look at you. We haven't got much time left... There's something I've wanted to tell you for so long... I..."
I love you too, Ye Sheng cut in simply and briskly. Then he did something the Executive Department might punish him for: he pressed his lips hard against Aki's and kissed her. She froze.

His mouth quirked, and there was that smile again, sometimes infuriating, sometimes enough to make her forget every worry in the world. Aki remembered floundering in the pool while Ye Sheng slapped his butt at her in the sunlight streaming through the floor-to-ceiling windows.
Idiot. Trust me. It's enough! Ye Sheng hugged Aki's slender body tight.
Hey, your legs aren't short at all, he told himself, and pulled her into the water in a headlong dive.
Faint whirlpools were forming in the water, a sign that an opening was appearing directly below.

Mans was dancing the cha-cha in the forward cabin, a rare lapse of dignity for Mans Rundstedt. But the captain was far too pleased with himself, delighted by his feat of snatching victory from disaster. His cherished students were coming home.

Now that's what I call a comeback! Mans twisted his hips and bragged to Selma. "Like a three-pointer at the last second of the fourth quarter! Like breaking every service game in the third set!" He glanced at his watch. "How many minutes left?"

He froze. His dance steps faltered, and he stumbled, nearly falling. Only a desperate grip on the wheel kept him upright. The color drained from his face. He shoved the door open and rushed outside to stand in the storm, staring blankly at the heaving river.
Captain? Selma and the first mate followed him out.

The exit is directly beneath the bronze city. They can get out of the city, but they won't have time to reach the surface. Mans's face twitched. "We calculated it wrong... Their oxygen... isn't enough!"
In the forward cabin, the Gate suddenly stopped crying. Tears welled in the baby's great wide eyes.

A buzzing came through the gale. Far away, an enormous pool of light moved across the black water. Moments later a hail came from off the port bow. "Attention, Moniach. This is the Yangtze Navigation Maritime Bureau. Respond with your lights. Respond with your lights."
The third mate came onto the deck. "Captain, do we keep waiting?"
Mans stared at the water, silent for several seconds, then looked down at his watch. Fourteen minutes had passed. Suddenly he felt tired.

Signal back. Accept their assistance. Evacuate everyone. He turned toward the cabin, then heard a dull thump from the stern. Instinctively he drew his flashlight and shone it over. Beside the lifeboat, a dark head surfaced, followed by a deathly pale face.
Aki! Mans could not believe his eyes.

His most beloved student, Aki Sakatoku, that Japanese girl who always radiated such maternal warmth, had somehow exceeded the limits of human diving and survived. She was struggling to push a brass jar almost as tall as herself into the lifeboat.
Selma! Selma! Get her out! Mans roared, then began swearing. "Get up here! Forget the damned jar! You Japanese are all obsessive maniacs!"

Aki did not answer him. She shouted something in Japanese and, with the last of her strength, shoved the brass jar into the lifeboat before looking up at Mans. She made no attempt to climb aboard. Her slender hand hooked around the rope along its side, and she gazed at Mans from far below.
Professor, take the jar and go! Go! she said hoarsely. "Ye Sheng... fought to bring it back..."

She went under. An immense force from beneath the water dragged her bodily down. Her long hair swirled once in the waves and vanished entirely. By the time Mans reached the rail, scarlet blood was welling up from below like a rising plume of red smoke.
Aki! Mans roared, savagely tearing open the buttons of his captain's uniform, ready to dive in.
Cut the anchors! Start the engines! Full boost! the third mate shouted too, hauling Mans back with all his strength.

He was the most seasoned sailor aboard, with more than ten years on the oceans. What had just happened to Aki was very strange, yet he had seen something like it before: a shark attacking a fellow diver. But sharks obviously did not live in freshwater, and judging by the immense whirlpool that had formed as Aki sank, this thing was astonishingly big.

Both anchor chains were cut at once. The powerful engines needed no warm-up; they started instantly. The tremendous acceleration sent the third mate and Mans tumbling together, clutching each other. In the instant before he fell, the third mate saw a sharp wake arrowing straight after them.
What is that? He broke into a cold sweat.
Get the sonar on! Find out what that thing is! Mans dragged the bronze jar into the cabin, his face twitching, murder written all over it.
Too fast for a precise image! About fifteen meters long. Looks like a fish! the second mate shouted.
A fish? the third mate said. "What fish can swim underwater at fifty knots?"
As long as it's alive. Mans clipped and lit a fresh cigar, then worked the muscles of his face hard. "If it's alive, it can die!"

Mans opened the weapons locker on the cabin wall. An L115A3 sniper rifle stood upright in the center. This British-made long-range weapon could be called the emperor of sniper rifles, but the Executive Department had still found its performance inadequate and optimized its ammunition. Mans loaded the magazine with cartridges that glinted cold blue, their bullets engraved with ancient patterns. Every primer was painted red, the distinctive mark of a high-risk weapon.
I really love those maniacs in the Executive Department who optimize our weapons! Mans slapped the magazine into the rifle.
Could it be the Dragon King? the third mate asked.
I hope so. Killing him is what I came for! Mans darted out of the cabin.

Xenon lights turned the foaming water behind the ship dazzling white, but the foam could not conceal that razor-sharp wake. It was as if an invisible blade were slicing through the surface from below. Mans leaned against the cabin wall and braced his feet on the rail, his whole body a drafting triangle wedged between wall and railing. It was the only way to keep his balance as the ship pitched violently. Through the infrared scope he saw the "fish" underwater. It was swimming at full speed, and its body temperature, far above that of the water, exposed it completely.
Very good, my boy, Mans said softly.

He squeezed the trigger. A straight streak of cold blue shot into the water, the tracer bullet heated by friction with the air. The report boomed like thunder. The enormous recoil could have knocked a strong man off his feet. The wake's advance suddenly faltered, and a whirlpool churned on the surface. Mans fired again and again, ten full rounds of large-caliber ammunition into the water. Before one blue streak faded, the next appeared. Several cold shafts of light hung in the black air at once, beautiful in their deadly severity. Watching the thing weave from side to side underwater as if trying to evade him, Mans took the cigar from his mouth and laughed hoarsely.
Selma! More ammunition! he roared.
He wanted to watch its corpse float up from the water. He wanted a good look at whatever had dared take his student from him a few meters away.

Selma rushed out with a freshly loaded magazine and saw the Maritime Bureau's helicopter hovering overhead. They had evidently noticed that something was pursuing the Moniach and trained their searchlight on the whirlpool in its wake. Bubbles surged up in the center. An impossibly huge black shape flashed into view, and for an instant Selma thought she was hallucinating. With incomparable power it broke through the surface and shot straight into the sky. At that moment lightning tore the sky apart, and in its glare the black shape twisted like a raging dragon. Selma's knees gave way, and she collapsed onto the deck. Countless lectures had taught her that this race existed in the world, but she had never once seen one reveal itself. It was a miracle: a dragon breaking out of the water and ascending into the sky. All this wind and rain had come to welcome this magnificent moment.

Mans snatched the magazine from her, slammed it into the rifle, and fired into the air. In an instant the creature reached the helicopter's height. Its upward momentum spent, it curled its long tail around the heavy helicopter's landing gear. It was certainly huge, yet hardly outsized beside an aircraft capable of carrying fifteen tons of cargo. Mans's bullets struck its body in little showers of sparks.

Using the landing gear as a springboard, the creature leaped again. Another bolt of lightning crossed the sky. In its glare, the creature's dragon-long body stretched out, paused for a fraction of a second, then twisted like a whip and lashed the helicopter's rotor. Steel fragments flew in every direction. The helicopter lost its balance and spiraled toward the river. Several dark figures threw open the cabin door and jumped. The helicopter struck the water with terrific force, throwing spray nearly fifty meters high. A dozen seconds later flames shot into the night sky. The helicopter had exploded underwater.
It... it took out a heavy helicopter? How can it leap twenty meters out of the water? Selma was dumbfounded.
We should accord him the courtesy of 'he.' He's an intelligent being, Mans said. "At this rate we're his next course."
The terrible wake reappeared, racing straight after the Moniach.
Would we taste that good...? The way it's chasing us, Selma asked.
What he really cares about... is probably that bronze jar. Mans shouted into the forward cabin, "What weapons do we have left?"

Only ten miniature underwater bombs! We're posing as a tug. We off-loaded the weapons to avoid trouble with inspections! the first mate roared back. He was at the helm, and with its engines on full boost, the Moniach hurtled like a maddened swordfish. Sweat kept beading on his forehead. Every scrap of his attention was on the complex instrument panels.
Because we weren't expecting to run into a fight! Ready the underwater bombs! Mans shouted.

The wheel spun rapidly in the first mate's hands. Throwing up spray nearly ten meters high, the Moniach cut a broad, zigzagging Z across the water. At the same time the second mate opened the underwater hatch and released all ten bombs in succession. Because of their Z-shaped course, the bombs formed three rows: three in front, four in the middle, three behind. Miniature engines activated, holding them suspended five to ten meters underwater. On the sonar monitor, they looked like a trap waiting for the creature.
Beautiful! the second mate said.

The placement was perfect. The creature would either have to slow down and go around, giving the Moniach time to escape, or get very intimate with the bombs. Miniature though they were, they were still products of those lunatics in the Equipment Department. When designing them, the lunatics had sincerely hoped that a single bomb would blast through the armor of a Los Angeles-class aircraft carrier.
Mans elbowed the second mate aside and leaned over the console. On the sonar screen, the shining dots and the enormous, vaguely fish-shaped creature drew closer and closer.
Very close! Fifty meters! the second mate shouted. "It's coming straight in! No deceleration!"
Good! Blow him to hell! Mans said.

The creature's cruising speed was close to the Moniach's, fifty knots. Fifty meters would vanish in two or three seconds, barely enough distance for an emergency stop. But what could brake to a halt in fifty meters underwater?
It... it stopped! The second mate went white.

They all strained their ears, waiting for a thunderous explosion, but the sonar showed the enormous creature stopped dead before the line of bombs. It was nothing like braking. There was no glide. In one abrupt movement it had become completely motionless, its speed dropping to zero. Not even a dolphin possessed such agility.
Detonate remotely? The second mate looked up at Mans.
Would it work?
Before you decide whether it'll work, maybe you should look at the screen... an intern ventured.

Five of the original ten dots had vanished. The enormous creature was circling the remaining ones, like a small whale curiously playing with a little school of jellyfish. Utterly bewildered, the second mate looked up at another monitor. It showed that five underwater bombs had lost their signals.
The last dot vanished before he could detonate the bombs.
Mans raised his head. "I think... your bombs got eaten."
Eaten...? A tremendous helplessness filled the second mate. "Would they taste good?" he suddenly asked, quite absurdly.
Captain... Selma's voice shook. She pointed astern.

Mans followed her finger. What pursued them was no longer a thin wake. A black spine had risen above the surface. They could dimly see each vertebra, jagged as a reef. Its long tail lashed at high speed without throwing up any spray. An immense mouth lay half submerged. Above the surface rose a hideous upper jaw, with two yellow-brown hooked fangs visible.
So it really is... a vertebrate, Mans murmured.
Reptiles are vertebrates, of course, Selma said, puzzled.
A great many theories about dragons are conjecture. Nobody knows for certain that they're reptiles. Perhaps what we call dragons are only shadows in the human heart, Mans said.
Captain! The bombs are transmitting again! the second mate shouted ecstatically, like a grieving father who had suddenly found his missing children.
Mans froze, then realized. "Quick! Detonate!"
That's strange. Weren't they... eaten? The second mate was bewildered.
But they haven't been digested! His body blocks electromagnetic waves, but now he's surfacing and opening his mouth! Your bombs are calling Daddy from his stomach! Mans slammed the detonation button.

A deafening explosion erupted a kilometer behind them, the shock of its roar making the entire Moniach tremble. As the ten underwater bombs detonated together, a vertical pillar of fire plunged into the water, like a sword of flame hurled down from the clouds by a god. An instant later the fire burst apart. Sharp metal fragments packed into the explosives sprayed in every direction; some struck the Moniach's stern.
We did it! Selma shouted, waving her arms. She had seen that black spine twist at the instant of the explosion. If it was still a living creature, there was no way it could have survived.

The Moniach swung through almost ninety degrees on the water and labored to a stop, its overheated engines boiling up clouds of steam beneath the hull. Everyone emerged from the cabins and stood in the storm, watching the water a kilometer away boil in an instant. An immense whirlpool spun on the surface, drawing great masses of foam into the depths. Mans wiped rain from his face and imagined the thick spine, whatever remained of it, slowly settling onto the riverbed. He let out a long breath.
If only we could capture a live specimen, the third mate sighed.
A live specimen fifteen meters long and weighing fifty tons. How would you get it back to Cassell College? Mans asked.
Was that the Dragon King Norton? Selma asked.

Probably not. A Dragon King wouldn't be stupid enough to eat bombs, Mans said. "In a little while we can go over and see if we can collect some tissue fragments for study back home. You did well this time, Selma. I'm giving you full marks for your field placement. Very few students in Cassell's history have managed that."
Selma nodded. "Thank you. Though right now I'd rather trade them for Ye Sheng and Aki."

Mans gripped her shoulder and squeezed hard. It was all the encouragement he could give her. Then he was jerked off balance. He froze. Selma slipped from his grasp and flew backward toward the water, as if an enormous demonic hand in the darkness had seized her by the back of her clothes. She sank straight down. A light swung toward her in the final instant, and Mans saw her mouth open wide without a sound, water pouring straight into it. She vanished. On the surface, only a slender black, snakelike shape curled once.
A long tail! The tail vertebrae that should already have been blown to pieces!
Mans snatched up the sniper rifle from the deck and emptied a whole magazine into the river. Moments later dark red blood rose to the surface.

He stood stunned. Suddenly he remembered that the monster was not the only thing underwater. Selma was there too. He did not know whether the blood was hers or the dragon's, but with fire that concentrated, even if Selma had still been alive, she would scarcely have escaped. He dropped the rifle and staggered backward a few steps, slumping against the cabin wall.
Uncanny laughter seemed to rise from the raging waves, echoing around the Moniach. It was very deep, yet carried a flippant delight.
Did you all hear that? the third mate asked, his voice shaking.
You heard correctly... The dragon is laughing. He's... laughing at us, Mans said quietly.

Rapid beeps sounded in the cabin. The second mate paused: the fire-control radar had reacquired a bomb's signal. One had been a dud in the detonation. Now a black spine slowly surfaced a short distance from the Moniach. The creature slowly opened its mouth. Everyone could see the dense beds of teeth extending nearly to its throat. Deep inside lay an underwater bomb blinking red.
Should we detonate again? the second mate asked.

He's waiting for you to do it, Mans said. "Remember the pillar of fire that shot upward during the explosion? That thing opened his mouth and pointed it skyward. All the hot gases from the explosion vented through his mouth, releasing the pressure, just like dragonfire. Now his mouth is pointed at us. Detonate it, and those hot gases will come straight at us."
Is his digestive tract made of iron? The second mate could not believe it.

I was wrong, Mans said quietly. "He's anything but stupid. He swallowed the bombs because he knew they couldn't hurt him. He probably attacked the helicopter because its lights annoyed him. He dodged my bullets because the harassment irritated him too. They couldn't hurt him. He's playing games with us, his cornered prey... Start the engines!"
They're already overheating. They won't hold out much longer, the chief engineer said.
We don't have to go far. Shine the lights ahead. See what's there, Mans said.
The first mate looked back and froze. In the darkness, they had thought only of flight, their sonar always scanning the pursuer astern. None of them had noticed the mountainlike shadow ahead.
The Three Gorges Dam.
Only a few kilometers separated them from this immense man-made structure that had cost tens of billions. The towering dam stood over the black water like a giant lying down to sleep.
There was nowhere left to run.
Back inside. Start the engines. Straight ahead, Mans said.
Everyone looked at him in silence.
I'm the captain. What I say goes here, Mans said. "Start the engines. Maximum power. Ahead!"

The overheated engines roared once more. Waves erupted at the stern, and the Moniach drove forward with her bow raised. Mans stood alone at the stern, watching the enormous creature circling in the distance. Rain ran swiftly down the wrinkles of his face.
Come on, he said softly.

As he had expected, the creature too had been waiting for this moment. Only when the prey began to flee would the final hunt begin. He suddenly submerged, and the razor wake reappeared. Nothing could interfere with him now. He closed in faster than ever before.
Navigation prohibited! Navigation prohibited! Approaching vessel, reduce speed immediately! came the lock operators' hail from atop the dam.

The Moniach's course was suicidal. All the locks had been closed because of the storm. The difference in elevation along the Three Gorges waterway was so great that there were five tiers of locks, with a twenty-meter drop between each. Even if the operators began filling the next lock immediately, they could not raise its level twenty meters in time. Opening the miter gates now would only release a flood. Immense volumes of water would thunder into the lock below, forming a spectacular, deadly torrent that would drag the tug in, carry it over the resulting waterfall, and smash it to pieces. If the gates stayed closed, a collision at this speed would smash it just as thoroughly. Each of those great gates had been cast from two thousand tons of steel.
Keep going! Mans's roar came from the stern.
The first mate's face was ashen, his hands steady on the wheel. The second mate rested his hand on the red detonation button. The creature had closed his mouth, and the signal had vanished again.

The third mate appeared in the forward cabin carrying the Key. Eyes wide, the Key stared straight at the miter gates drawing ever closer through the night. He reached out his tiny hand and pointed into empty air ahead. His little body trembled, and pale gold flowed through his eyes. An immense power surged from his hand. Everyone felt it.

With a crash, the miter gates parted down the middle! The Key's Yanling forced a passage open. Living spirits were not the only things he could command; the Three Gorges waterway's safety systems obeyed him too.

An enormous volume of water poured into the lower lock. The torrent immediately dragged the Moniach in, and her speed reached an unprecedented seventy knots. They accelerated toward death, toward a twenty-meter waterfall. Amid the chaotic currents, the Moniach could no longer hold her heading. One moment the entire vessel swung broadside, the next she shot forward like an arrow. The creature sensed danger and slowed down.

Mans opened the ancient pewter flask in his hand. It had slept for thousands of years in an Egyptian tomb before Cassell College spent a fortune acquiring it at auction. The seller had not understood its true value, but Cassell's people had. They had painted the whole flask red for "high risk" and stored it with great care in the Ice Cellar. Mans poured its liquid over the bronze jar beside him, which he had lashed to himself with a cable.

The corrosive effect was immediate and violent. Where the gray liquid touched the jar, it bubbled incessantly like concentrated acid. It crawled along the patterns on the bronze surface like tiny gray snakes, frantically seeking gaps to enter. The jar was about to open.

The dragon in the water gave a piercing shriek. What Mans was doing had clearly driven him into a fury. He stopped fighting the currents, curved his spine like a bow, plunged beneath the surface, and lunged toward the Moniach.
Everyone fasten your safety harnesses! the first mate roared.
Ahead! He shoved the throttle all the way forward.

Carried by the torrent, the Moniach "flew" out of the first lock, passed through the miter gates, and hung briefly in the air. The first mate heard the engine race without resistance and cut out. He had done everything he could, just as Mans had ordered. He did not want to die slaying dragons, but he had prepared himself for the day if it ever came. He closed his eyes.
Beep, beep, beep: the signal from the final bomb. The second mate slammed the detonator!

A terrible sight was reflected in Mans's pupils. An immense mouth gaped as it rushed toward him, its two yellow-brown, saber-curved fangs a full meter long, its rows of teeth dense as thorns! Half his body was still inside the lock, but he had thrust his head eagerly out. His long black body lay half concealed in the night, its countless scales glimmering faintly.
A violent explosion erupted inside the creature. Flame gushed forth like an oversized welding torch.
A string of explosive syllables spilled from Mans's mouth.
Yanling: Dustless Realm.

He issued his command within the domain. Immense air pressure drove outward from its center, forcing back bomb fragments and searing flames alike. In a flash a spherical barrier appeared around Mans, shielding him from the blast. Outside it, the scorching wind softened even steel. The shock wave threw the creature back, forcing half his body to recoil into a coil.
In the third mate's arms, the Key suddenly clenched his tiny hand!

The miter gates' motors started at once, and the two-thousand-ton steel gates slammed shut. The immense fifteen-meter body was caught across the middle. A wild, piercing laugh stabbed out of the torrent like a sword. Mans covered his ears. He had never heard laughter like it. Laughter, yes, but also something like an agonized death wail.

Mans did not know whether the creature was showing fearless defiance in the face of death, or whether he was simply incapable of making any sound that did not resemble laughter. He no longer cared. He had killed the bastard. This was his offering to his students' memory.
Farewell, Your Highness Norton. Cold mockery flashed in Mans's bloodshot eyes.
The Moniach plunged straight down with the torrent toward the water in the second lock. Mans smiled without a sound.
Utter silence filled the control room in Cassell College's library.
The Moniach's signal had cut out. The screen was black. Half an hour had passed. Professor Schneider rubbed his hands and paced. Waiting like this made it impossible to sit still.

Lu Mingfei was probably the only one who did not find time dragging: he was in the middle of a fierce battle. EVA had suggested a game of StarCraft. He knew getting caught playing StarCraft at a time like this would be a truly shameful business, but EVA seemed to be finding the wait unbearable. The virtual girl kept pacing from one end of the screen to the other, hopping, scratching her head, and idly drawing circles on the floor. Then she suggested, "How about a one-on-one?" Lu Mingfei felt that no man could refuse.

It had been a while, but fortunately he had not lost his touch. With a mouse in his hand, Lu Mingfei owned the world. He was Zerg as usual: a perfect opening scout, Zergling harassment, Hydralisks, level-one attack and armor, an expansion. It all flowed effortlessly.

EVA's style was completely different from Nono's. She did not go for explosive rushes. She chose Protoss and immediately placed Photon Cannons outside her base, with a squad of upgraded Zealots guarding the gun line. Lu Mingfei did not recklessly charge his Hydralisks in. He realized EVA must be up to something. She was a computer's virtual personality; peeking at the map would be no trouble at all. She had already used that trick when partnering with Nono.
You've been looking at my map again, haven't you? Lu Mingfei typed.

I have. But I only have one mineral field and one geyser. You've already built six expansions, with twelve Hatcheries in all. You can produce three squads of Hydralisks at once, EVA said. "Max out your attack and armor. Then our game begins."
What?
I attack you head-on. We'll see how many waves you can hold out against, EVA said.

Who knew a pretty girl like you was into going so hard on the offensive! You won't cheat and raise your supply cap? Lu Mingfei suddenly felt eager. What other computer could give you a game this exhilarating, and chat with you while it was at it?
No. Two hundred supply maximum. Fair and square, EVA said. "Begin!"
The moment she finished speaking, Lu Mingfei saw a tidal wave of Zealots pour out of EVA's lines!
If you're a man, survive ten waves! EVA said.
If you're a little girl, don't run away! Lu Mingfei was delighted with this new way to play.

What followed was the most exhausting tug-of-war of his life. A computer like EVA never had to worry about command: every unit maneuvered independently, flanking and circling. Lu Mingfei fought back ferociously with a full supply of Hydralisks and turrets everywhere. EVA had set his minerals and gas to infinity. Around twenty Hatcheries across the screen spewed Hydralisks at a frantic rate, sending them converging on the central battlefield. These versatile units were good against air and ground alike, and when one was nearly dead, he could morph it into a Lurker. EVA fielded different units in each wave: Zealots, Dragoons, Scouts, Corsairs, swarms of Reavers... Relying on the Zerg's unrivaled production speed, Lu Mingfei held off nine waves in succession. By the time he cleared out three squads of Carriers in the last one, he had only half a squad of wounded Hydralisks left.
Come on. I'm ready. Lu Mingfei replenished his supply, and his Defilers and Queens were back at full energy too.
Wave ten, EVA said.

Carriers? Dragoons? Or swarms of Archons? As Lu Mingfei waited eagerly, the screen suddenly went black, with only faint dark markings drifting across it. He pressed Enter. Amazingly, chat still worked.
EVA, did you crash? he typed.
No. The game is still going. Want me to pull the camera back a little?
Camera? What camera?

Suddenly he could make out the enemy on the screen. EVA was right: only by "pulling the camera back" could this enemy be seen. For the final wave, EVA had only one unit, a black dragon so vast it blotted out everything, spreading its wings as it glided slowly past. It breathed fire, and every Hydralisk in its path dissolved into bloody pulp. The screen had not gone black. The dragon was many times larger than the area the screen could display, and those dark markings Lu Mingfei had seen were its scales.
That's one big guy! Lu Mingfei exclaimed aloud.
The Black Dragon King Nidhogg. His name means 'despair,' EVA said. "You lose. Let's play again sometime, Lu Mingfei."
The screen flickered and switched back to the utterly unappealing work interface.
Big guy? Professor Schneider frowned. "What big guy?"
Lu Mingfei sprang to his feet. "'Big guy' means quiet in Chinese slang... I meant, it's so quiet!"

Professor Schneider nodded slightly. Lu Mingfei had voiced what they were all feeling. It was indeed too quiet. The black screen, the silent speakers, as if... everything were dead. He had a vague, ominous premonition, but could not speak of it to anyone. It seemed that the moment he said it aloud, it would come true.
One very big guy indeed! Mans... how are you doing? He let out a long sigh.

The main screen suddenly lit up, and an old man's serene face appeared. His silvery-white hair was combed with meticulous care. Time had left deep marks on his face, turning his skin into the cracked bark of an ancient tree or weathered rock, but its lines remained firm, and light danced in his silver-gray eyes. An immaculate black suit clothed his still-erect figure. A vivid red rose stood in his breast pocket.
For a moment Lu Mingfei could not guess his age. By his skin and features, he was very, very old, yet he sat like a young lion.
So cool! Lu Mingfei marveled. "The ultimate old guy!"
Everyone rose to their feet at once.
Principal Anjou, Professor Schneider said.
The Moniach has landed safely in the second lock of the Three Gorges Reservoir. We have acquired valuable information. Thank you all for your efforts. You are dismissed, the principal said calmly.

The control room erupted. Everyone raised their arms and cheered. Professors embraced in their excitement; students high-fived. The students were clearly split into two camps, however: one clustered around Caesar, the other around Chu Zihang. At this crucial moment Kiran had hurried off to the restroom. Lu Mingfei was left alone, some distance from everybody, unsure which group he should join.
Then he saw Nono leaning alone against the wall, chewing gum and staring absently out the window.
Suddenly he felt happy. There was still Nono in this world, on the same side as him.
Hey! Lu Mingfei! You're the best! Kiran was back, actually carrying a bouquet. He came over, shook Lu Mingfei's hand vigorously, then wrapped him in a powerful hug.

The control room fell quiet for a moment. The professors began to applaud. The elite members of the Lionheart Society and Student Council looked to their respective presidents. Caesar and Chu Zihang began clapping too, and then everybody joined in. In an instant Lu Mingfei was surrounded by people shaking his hand, blocking his view of Nono. As he experienced respect for the first time, he saw Nono outside the crowd glance at him indifferently and go on blowing a bubble. The bubble grew bigger and bigger, then finally burst.
Dismissed! Professor Schneider announced.
The students left the control room, waving to the principal on the screen. Clearly he enjoyed idol status here. He only smiled, without answering.
But as Lu Mingfei reached the door, he heard the principal say behind him, "Thank you, Lu Mingfei."

Surprised, Lu Mingfei turned. On the screen the principal raised a sheaf of white paper. "Congratulations. You have passed the 3E exam with the highest score in ten years. You have retained your S-rank status, and I will award you a special Principal's Scholarship."

Professors and students exchanged astonished glances. After decades, another "true" S-rank student had appeared at Cassell College. This boy who looked like the world's most hopeless loser had demonstrated what his rank meant through both his score and his extraordinary ability.
The peerless S-rank.
Don't let that bubble pop! Nono brushed past Lu Mingfei, patted his shoulder, and walked out.
An excited Professor Guderian came up and shook his hand hard. "The Principal's Scholarship! It's the college's highest honor! Mingfei, I always had faith in you!"

Lu Mingfei felt a little lost. When Nono had patted him just now, he had not understood her expression. Whatever it was, it certainly was not happy. There had been a chill in it. Had S-rank offended her somehow?
As the students emerged from the library, the church bell began to ring.

Lu Mingfei found it strange. He had been at the college for several days, and the church bell had never rung even once. But now it swung again and again, its deep tolling going on and on like a stubborn old man.

Everyone stopped and raised their heads toward the bell tower. A great flock of white doves poured out, calling and circling in the air, hundreds or thousands of them. At last white wings covered the sky above the lawn. Caesar reached up, and a dove alighted on his finger. Then all the doves settled on the grass. They did not forage, only cooed, and there was something mournful in the sound.

One by one, the students who had been beaming a moment ago fell silent. Caesar took a white pocket square from his uniform and tied it to the railing beside the lawn. The other students did the same, until the railing looked like a tree blooming with white flowers.
In his bewilderment, Lu Mingfei heard someone behind him say, "Someone has left us."
He turned and saw Chu Zihang's pale gold eyes. The president of the Lionheart Society had actually spoken to him first.
Whenever someone leaves us, the church releases doves. It's a mourning rite, Chu Zihang said softly, watching the lawn.
He was S-rank and Chu Zihang only A-rank, yet speaking to a student leader like this, Lu Mingfei felt like a little underling, obliged to nod hard.
Chu Zihang patted his shoulder and smiled faintly. "Thank you. Without you deciphering that map, more people would have left us."

Lu Mingfei had never imagined Chu Zihang could smile. He always wore the same expressionless face, even when Lu Mingfei had shot him flat. His lack of expression differed from Caesar's aloofness: Caesar was proud, while Chu Zihang seemed indifferent to everything. But now he was smiling, gentle as an older brother.
Is your younger brother doing well? Chu Zihang asked.
He's... doing fine, Lu Mingfei said. "He really looks up to you."
Chu Zihang smiled again, politely rather than happily.
You're not afraid to meet my eyes, are you? he said.
No.
That's good. There aren't many eyes I get to look into, actually. People don't like me meeting their gaze.

Lu Mingfei suddenly understood why Chu Zihang always kept his eyelids lowered and his face expressionless. Those golden eyes that never went dark inspired involuntary fear in others. He had been avoiding people's gazes. Now they were fully open to Lu Mingfei, beautiful in an uncanny way.
This is my formal invitation. Join the Lionheart Society, Chu Zihang said. "You will be the next president after me. I promise."
Why? Lu Mingfei froze.

Handing out offices and promises already? Wasn't this a little fast? He hadn't even defected to the Nationalists yet, and they were making him a major general? No, this was practically naming him the next Generalissimo!
Because whoever succeeds me must be someone who can stand against me, Chu Zihang said.

Lu Mingfei lowered his head and scratched the back of his neck. This was his second invitation today. In the library, Kiran had already announced that, as acting president of the Freshman Association, he had finally found its truly suitable president: Lu Mingfei. It had frightened Lu Mingfei into waving both hands frantically.

Actually, stepping aside for him as president of the Freshman Association was at least understandable. He had no talent, but his S-rank could pay his way. President of the Lionheart Society, though... wasn't that taking the joke a little far? It was Cassell College's oldest club, and its leader's position was something Caesar had coveted for ages. Caesar had joined the Student Council only because the previous Lionheart leader disliked his arrogance. What had Lu Mingfei ever done to deserve something even Caesar could not get?

He wanted very sincerely to crack some stupid joke: Your Majesty, your kindness overwhelms this unworthy servant; the imperial throne isn't something you can just abdicate at the drop of a hat! But he did not dare say it. Chu Zihang looked straight into his eyes, calm but serious, like a capable young king who meant every word he said.
Caesar will be hoping you'll join the Student Council too. If you choose them, that's fine as well, Chu Zihang said calmly. "Someone like you would make me happy as either a friend or an opponent."
He lowered his eyelids, patted Lu Mingfei's shoulder, and turned away.

Lu Mingfei stood there dumbly for a long time before finally letting out a breath. He was drenched in cold sweat. What did he mean, "happy as either a friend or an opponent"? That was a threat, right? A naked threat? Could anyone make a threat that calmly? It was like a girl smiling through narrowed eyes and saying, "If I can't love you, I'd rather kill you!"

At the Three Gorges Reservoir, a black helicopter hovered above the lock. On the heaving water, the Moniach floated belly-up. She had capsized on impact, and everything above her waterline was submerged in the icy river. A ladder descended from the helicopter, and a tall, slender dark figure climbed down. With his back to the light, he held a black umbrella against the rain.
Mans struggled to raise his head for a look at the figure. A sodden cigar between his teeth, he managed a difficult smile. "Principal."

The baby in his arms was bawling. Apart from that, there was only the endless storm, not another human voice. His closest comrades floated in the icy river. Young Selma had never had the chance to receive the full marks she had earned. At the instant of impact, the third mate had curled around the Key, shielding the baby with his body. His own spine had broken.

Principal Anjou crouched beside Mans, took out a lighter, and lit the cigar in his mouth. Then he examined the wound at his waist. A yellow-brown tooth had pierced him there. In the violent explosion a section of fang had snapped off and flown through the air. Dustless Realm had failed to stop it.
A little higher and I wouldn't have lasted until you got here. Mans drew deeply on the cigar.
Principal Anjou pressed a hand to his wound. "Don't talk. A doctor will be down at once."

The principal was very old, but his hand was still warm and strong. Mans felt a little life flow back into his body. He grinned. "A doctor won't help. Let me finish my last report, like the heroes in movies."
Yes, a doctor won't help. Dragon fangs contain a powerful venom. It's attacking your nervous system. You can't be saved. The principal nodded. "Then begin at once."

Mans handed him the baby. His other hand had never loosened its death grip on a rope, not even while he was unconscious. He handed that over too. The principal pulled the submerged bronze jar up by the rope, stroked the intricate patterns on its surface, and recited softly.

I think I killed the Dragon King Norton. Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku brought this bronze jar out of the underground bronze palace. I don't know what's inside, but Norton wanted it back badly. It should have considerable research value. You should search upstream in the reservoir for the dragon's remains. There may still be time to extract DNA. Nothing else, really. I know I have an insurance policy that covers flying my body back to Germany... Mans forced himself to the end, his strength already failing.

It wasn't the Dragon King Norton. Only a dragon servitor, a warrior guarding the Dragon King's soul, the principal said. "This jar is a bone vessel, or an 'egg.' Its inscription reads: 'I offer my bones and blood to the great sovereign Nidhogg, the supreme, the almighty, the all-virtuous, who rules the world through destiny.' Norton is inside this!"
Was he the one behind Gongsun Shu? Mans asked.
We'll know after we've studied it. When we have the answer, would you like us to carve it on your headstone? the principal asked.

No need. Just my wife's name will do, Mans said. "Don't tell the students that the entire Operation Kuimen team was wiped out. For them, this sort of thing is still a long way off. They needn't grieve for us. They should still believe dragon slaying is exciting and full of passion, something worth devoting their lives to."
How good that would be, Mans said softly.

I haven't told them. They only know Ye Sheng and Aki have left us. I was very calm, the principal said. "I just don't know how I'll keep the lie going once I'm back on campus. Who's going to cover your classes? You still have courses this semester."

Schneider. He really wants to keep teaching. Mans exhaled smoke through his nostrils. "Tell them we've gone on a new assignment. The world's a big place, after all, with dragon ruins everywhere. You can always say they're busy on another expedition. After a few years, it won't really matter whether you announce it or not."
All right. We'll do as you say.
Goodbye. Say hello to Nono for me. She'll need a new adviser. The cigar fell into the water, and Mans slowly closed his eyes.

The principal drew the rose, just about to bloom, from his breast pocket and laid it on Mans's chest. Then he stood with the bawling baby in his arms. Lights converged from every direction. Searchlights shone on him; military and police vehicles lined both riverbanks. Silently, the old man straightened, patted the baby's cheek, tucked the little head against his chest, and raised the black umbrella over himself.
What a big guy, Professor Manstein said softly. On the library's second floor, he watched the students below gradually disperse, leaving only the white pocket squares tied all along the railing.
Big guy? Professor Guderian paused.

A Chinese dialect expression. It means silence. Manstein took off his glasses, deeply moved. "A new semester. Some have left us, the freshmen haven't grown up yet, and we're already old. It really makes a man feel... big guy."

Yes. Very big guy, Guderian said, moved as well. "There's something I'm curious about. You stopped doubting Lu Mingfei before you knew his 3E score. I hear you even bet online that he'd pass. What are you hiding from me?"
I'd never hide anything from you. Aren't we good friends from the same mental hospital? Manstein shrugged.
That sounds a little odd...

It's simply the truth. I stopped doubting Lu Mingfei—Manstein pointed at the distant bell tower—"because I called my father. He said there was no reason to doubt him: Lu Mingfei was the finest of all dragon-blood descendants."
The Night Watcher said that? Guderian exclaimed.
Yes. But he offered no explanation.
Guderian gazed at the bell tower that never opened to visitors. "I always find it hard to think of the Night Watcher as your father. You don't look like someone who ought to have a father."

He made life miserable for my mother and me. I never had a childhood at all. I can't say I feel any family affection for him... But as a dragon slayer, he's probably the only man in the world who can compare with the principal, Manstein said. "There are still some things I trust him on. At least... thanks to him, I cleaned up in the betting pool!"
Lu Mingfei lay in bed listening to the rustle of paper from the upper bunk, over and over, back and forth, without end.
Hey! Brother Deadbeat, he said.
I'm busy. Unless it's important, shut up. For once Fingel sounded serious.
You're just reading. Can't we talk? Would talking kill you? Lu Mingfei said.
Since when is reading important? The rustling continued above.
Lu Mingfei craned his neck for a look at the upper bunk. "Hey! Could you be any more outrageous?"

The upper bunk was piled with U.S. currency. Fingel was counting stacks of bills, wearing a positively Père Goriot smile. Each time he finished a stack, he tore a strip from the philosophy book he claimed to cherish most and tied it around the bills.

Perfectly legitimate. I won it. Didn't rob a bank, Fingel said. "I knew you had talent. My little prince of good luck! You'd bring me luck! If Manstein hadn't bet on the same side, I'd have won even more."
'Little prince of good luck' is the most nauseating name ever! Hey, there's something I haven't figured out. Got time to explain? Lu Mingfei said.
For a bowl of cream soup, the Cassell College Yellow Pages will provide the most comprehensive answers available. Fingel patted his chest. "That's me."
Bandit! Lu Mingfei grabbed the phone. "Two cream soups with puff-pastry crusts! And I want a big slice of cheesecake!"
Fingel clapped his hands.
Did someone really... die? Lu Mingfei asked.
Actually, the casualty list's already been posted. Executive Department: Ye Sheng, Aki Sakatoku, Fingel said. "You can check the message board."
Lu Mingfei fell silent. He still remembered Aki Sakatoku smiling and correcting his pronunciation: "Ohayō." How could someone just suddenly die?

Don't worry too much. The Executive Department isn't necessarily that dangerous. Most of the time they're like an archaeological team, flying all over the world exploring dragon ruins. In the past ten years, I think there've only been a few deaths from passage collapses while they were raiding tombs. This time was exceptional, Fingel said. "The bronze city was the Dragon King Norton's tomb. Dragon tombs really are dangerous. There's a legend that any team that enters one has to sacrifice at least one member. An offering. But all missions into dragon tombs are classified, and nobody knows the whole story, so it's only a legend."
Have you ever worried about dying? Lu Mingfei asked.
Fingel thought for a moment. "Do you worry about finding a caterpillar in your burger?"
Obviously!

Then of course I worry about dying. It's a perfectly normal reaction, okay? Fingel shrugged. "Everyone comes to Cassell for their own reasons. They're all different. But when you get down to it, a lot of people here hate their dragon blood."
Hate their dragon blood? How? You all look cooler than the next guy!
Do you know why Manstein and Guderian are such inseparable buddies? They graduated from the same mental hospital. Fingel raised his eyebrows.
Wait! Lu Mingfei froze. "What... mental hospital?"

Hybrids don't think like ordinary people. It's hard for them to fit in. Guderian and Manstein showed extraordinary abilities as children, so people thought they were mentally ill and kept them locked in a hospital until they were fifteen. That's why Cassell College calls itself another choice. Choose Cassell, and you have to say goodbye to ordinary life. Here, the only thing you can do is slay dragons. Because the beings dragons hate most are precisely dragon hybrids. We have a dragon's abilities, but we're human inside. We live in the cracks between two worlds, welcome in neither.
Right! Lu Mingfei looked thoughtful. "You really aren't human."
You're not human! Your whole family isn't human...
You have a point... If my parents belong to the college too, they ought to have dragon tails as well. Lu Mingfei actually agreed.

Fingel was used to this junior's skin being thicker than a city wall. His own was hardly thin. "Take Chu Zihang. Everybody here says he's all bottled up. He's always kept himself under tight control, hiding how different he is from ordinary people. From high school on, he searched the entire internet for information on dragons. He's one of the few people in recent years who contacted Cassell on their own initiative. At first they couldn't believe a hybrid with such pure dragon blood could exist. So he must have had an incredibly repressed childhood. Now he's found his people, of course he's going to throw himself into dragon slaying!"
What about Caesar? He's not bottled up at all. He flaunts it.

Caesar's the exception. His full name is Caesar Gattuso. The Gattusos are a famous Italian noble family. They've produced seven or eight dukes, but unfortunately none ever made it onto Italy's imperial throne. The family always thought they ought to produce an emperor. Then they discovered that even as a small child Caesar had tremendous leadership qualities and a gift for mathematics and fighting. His logical thinking was very different from other children's, and the Gattuso elders were overjoyed, Fingel said. "Caesar flaunts it because the elders in his family adored him too much."
Lucky bastard. Nobody thought being such a pompous blowhard was a mental illness too? Lu Mingfei was not fond of Caesar.
An emperor! His family expects him to become an emperor. Emperors are bound to be different from ordinary people. It would be strange if they weren't.
An emperor? In this day and age?

The Gattusos were deeply disappointed! They waited hundreds of years for someone who could become emperor of Italy, and what happened? Democracy. No more emperors. They had to lower their sights to prime minister. Caesar graduated from Eton. Top universities fought to admit him. Between Cambridge and Cassell, he chose Cassell. He didn't come here for consolation. He thought it offered more of a challenge, something suited to a freakishly powerful guy like him. The first thing he said on enrolling was, 'You may challenge me, but I'm already prepared to laugh at you!'
Lu Mingfei covered his face. "What was the first thing I said when I enrolled?"
If we count from the moment you boarded the train, I remember it was... 'Holy crap, this is fancy!'
Who knew that seedpod head of yours had such a good memory! Lu Mingfei thought for a moment. "What about my senior?"

Your senior? Aren't we affectionate! Unfortunately, these Yellow Pages contain no history of the girlfriend of Caesar whom you're lusting after. She seems to have a very rich dad, but she always tells people she has no family. She has a younger brother, also of dragon blood, who never grows up. His name's Gates, nicknamed 'the Key,' just the opposite of his name. The little guy's blood can open every door in the world. An eager expression came over Fingel's face. "I often think, if I ever get so poor I have to rob a bank, I'll ask him to help."
I've seen her driving a Ferrari!
I've seen her driving a Lamborghini. But strangely enough, she still works a campus job with Guderian. You'd think she'd have no need to earn money herself. Anyway, be careful getting close to her.
Why? Lu Mingfei paused.

Know her nicknames? 'Red-haired Nono,' or 'the Red-haired Witch.' Fingel looked mysterious. "Sometimes she's very quiet, sometimes she's completely wild. If you try using your privilege of courting any girl for three months without being rejected, she might actually say yes!"
And Caesar would beat me to a pulp, wouldn't he?

Back in the day, our good buddy Paris, second prince of Troy, risked a joint pulping by Agamemnon and Achilles to carry dear Helen back to his palace. What are you afraid of? Fingel declared grandly. "Besides, Caesar's a true hero. Brothers are your own limbs; women are only clothes!"
Pah! Lu Mingfei suddenly remembered something. "Oh, Chu Zihang talked to me today!"

I know. The whole college knows! Fingel brought over his laptop and connected to Cassell's campus homepage. The lead story read: "S vs. A! A Gaze Brimming with Feeling!" In the accompanying photograph, two boys smiled into each other's eyes in the afternoon sunlight, a faint light reflected in their gazes. One was Lu Mingfei, king of the freshmen; the other was Chu Zihang, president of the Lionheart Society.
Lu Mingfei covered his face again. "Does this college have paparazzi too? Are they going to question my orientation?"
Absolutely not! The second story sets your orientation straight.

Lu Mingfei opened the second story. Its photograph showed the little look on his face as he stared at Nono's back while she pulled him at a run toward the library... Even Lu Mingfei wanted to slap the boy in the picture twice. The headline read: "A Gaze as Deep as the Sea! Boyfriends, Rest Easy: S-rank Has Found His Target!"
'Deep as the sea,' my ass! Lu Mingfei nearly jumped up. "Which paparazzo wrote this? They're trying to get me killed!"
Come to think of it, probably one of my boys, Fingel said thoughtfully.
Brother Evil Mastermind! Can you delete it? There's still time if Caesar hasn't seen it! Lu Mingfei looked miserable. "Please!"

Maybe Caesar hasn't seen it himself, but... he has so many boys, the ones who saw it will have sent him screenshots already... Delete it now and it'll only look worse. Fingel comforted him. "Public figures needn't fear romantic gossip. It's like a male monkey: if he's capable enough, he can monopolize a whole troop of females."
What kind of comparison is that?
Monkey social relationships have things in common with human ones, you know. Fingel waggled his eyebrows.

Stop! Lu Mingfei waved sharply. "Forget everything else! Listen! The problem now is, Chu Zihang invited me to join the Lionheart Society and said I'd be the next president after him, and if I don't join he'll... Never mind. Then there's Kiran. Kiran says I ought to join the Freshman Association as president. Do you have to pledge allegiance to some gang when you enter this college? Can you survive if you don't? Which gang is easiest to pledge allegiance to?"
Fingel rolled his eyes up toward the ceiling, as if this were an immensely difficult question requiring lengthy consideration.

He got up and paced a few steps. "Strategically speaking, deciphering that map was far too spectacular. Highest score in 3E history, a Principal's Scholarship: you've become much too famous. If this were the Middle Ages, a promising young dragon slayer like you would already have been knighted. So every faction is trying to recruit you. The Freshman Association is offering to make you its boss. That's easy enough to understand. The freshmen don't want to be caught between the Lionheart Society and Student Council. Both are after new recruits. Once the Freshman Association's members get split up, they'll have to become each other's opponents. Kiran has some organizational skills, but he isn't as impressive as you. He lacks your leadership charisma."
Leadership charisma? Me? Lu Mingfei hung his head.

By comparison, Chu Zihang's offer is even more attractive. He wants to groom you as his successor. The Lionheart Society originally ranked above the Student Council at the college. Its president is almost always the most gifted young person. I hear the principal's big brother Meinhard was its first president. So everyone thinks the principal is pretty partial to it. Becoming its president would be a fine start to your heroic career!

Pah! What heroic career? Have you lost your mind? Right now I'm just figuring out how to stay alive here. Lu Mingfei rolled his eyes. "Other people may not know, but you should. Don't you know how I passed the 3E exam? The map... that's hard to explain. Anyway, it wasn't anything I could do. It's all fake! You stick two wooden Mauser pistols in your belt and think you're ready to head into the hills and be a bandit king? All I want to know is whose coattails I should cling to."

You really do have a born collaborator's attitude. Come on, are you Liu Shan? You're about to make a name for yourself. They're inviting you to be the boss, not some little running dog. Anyway, of the three major clubs, only Caesar's Student Council hasn't invited you, and you're secretly lusting after his girlfriend...
Hey! Not lusting! It's 'having a favorable impression of a dashing senior'! Lu Mingfei said hastily.

Caesar may be a campus politician who knows how to take risks—a true hero, as the Chinese say. But a hero only has one good set of clothes. Caesar won't want to go bare-assed, much less share them with you. If you want a comfortable life, you have no choice but to cling to Chu Zihang's big, sturdy coattails. You did go to the same high school, after all. Fingel ignored him completely.
Lu Mingfei scratched his head hard. This decision would determine how easily he got by in the future. It was a terrible dilemma.
The laptop chimed to announce a new email. Lu Mingfei opened it and froze.
Ricardo:
There's a dinner and dance at Amber Hall tomorrow evening at 6:00. Come have something to eat if you're free. Caesar says he'd like to talk to you.
Remember to wear formal clothes. Friendly reminder: your uniform doesn't count. You can rent something from the college theater.
Nono
Fingel leaned over for a look and stared dumbly for a while too. "Liu Shan... Sima Zhao's come to invite you dancing... Now all three clubs want a piece of you."
Lu Mingfei raised his head. "Senior, now... which kingdom should I surrender to?"

Night fell, and Amber Hall lit up. Through its enormous floor-to-ceiling windows, the lights inside blazed in dazzling colors. The villa had Gothic spires, a roof of deep red tiles, and walls faced in Indian granite. Student Council officers stood beneath the covered walkway welcoming guests, dressed in black formal suits with white handkerchiefs or deep red roses tucked into their breast pockets.
Sweet mother of mercy! Caesar's house could fit a hundred of us! Hidden in a distant clump of bushes, Lu Mingfei clicked his tongue in admiration. "Capitalist society really does eat people alive."

Caesar doesn't live here all the time. He rents it for Student Council activities. He used to pay no rent—he won the right to use Norton Hall every year... Now Norton Hall belongs to you. Fingel wore a black formal suit. He was actually a big, tall man; it was only his soul that was a little seedy. Dressed like this, with his broad shoulders and long arms, his German gray brows and eyes, and his unruly hair tied into a little ponytail to reveal a rather handsome forehead, he looked every inch a bodyguard standing behind Lu Mingfei.
Then why don't we move into Norton Hall? Lu Mingfei suddenly remembered.

First you'd have to spend ten thousand dollars or so fixing up the furniture. Then there are the enormous heating bills and property taxes... If you're willing to pay, I'd be delighted to move in. I'd even be delighted to share your bed if you asked.
Get lost!
Then I'll get lost now. Give Caesar my regards. Fingel turned to go.
Senior, your loyalty knows no bounds. You absolutely have to go through this with me. Looking miserable, Lu Mingfei grabbed him.

Hah! Telling me to get lost? Fingel rolled his eyes. "Take a good look. This is going to be a tough one. They've spent serious money! His boys are all wearing Armani or Zegna suits, Montblanc or Vacheron Constantin watches. Every car out front is an Aston Martin or a Jaguar..." He shook his own obviously too-small formal jacket, which could barely contain him. "Compare that with our two rented outfits... I think Caesar's planning to flaunt his wealth at you. Either that or slap dollar bills in your face and say, 'Either come conquer the world with me or start licking my shoes!'"
I hope his feet don't stink...
Have you no dignity? Fingel covered his face. "Huh? New development!"

The reporters waiting outside Amber Hall clicked away at their cameras. The focus of their flashes and attention was a pickup backing toward the main entrance, carrying something beneath a thick tarpaulin. Student Council officers whipped the tarp away. Scarlet poured from the truck bed like a waterfall, a streak of color breathtaking against the overcast evening sky.
Thousands upon thousands of roses, freshly picked and still wet with dew, spilled before Amber Hall like rivers pouring into the sea.
Caesar even prepared roses for you. Look how he loves and values you! Fingel marveled.
Values your sister!
I don't have a sister! Fingel said.
Then he values mine? someone said behind them.

Lu Mingfei and Fingel turned together. A girl stood behind them in a deep purple skirt suit, a little moon-white silk blouse, purple stockings, and a full set of custom gold jewelry set with amethysts. Her dark red hair was immaculately combed, and she wore Mary Jane heels ten centimeters high. She held a pitch-black umbrella. Rain streamed off its rim, making her seem enclosed in a veil.
Somehow Nono had come to stand behind them.
Huh? Has the lady of the house come out to greet her guests in person? Fingel said, taken aback.

I've come to catch thieves! What are you two sneaking around for? Come with me! Nono closed her umbrella, seized Lu Mingfei with one hand and Fingel with the other, and dragged them straight toward Amber Hall's entrance.

Amid his confusion, Lu Mingfei heard clear, measured, forceful applause. Turning his head, he saw Caesar in white formal dress at the end of the walkway, his hair gleaming like gold. Rhinestones studded the lace cravat at his collar, and a cool, austere smile touched his lips. It was impossible to tell whether it meant welcome or mockery.
